passage: I'm Charu, Naveen's older sister. Three days before Diwali, Naveen had plans: cricket with friends, then a film. Instead Ma handed him a duster and the fan-cleaning job. He grumbled all morning, loud enough for the neighbours, and banged the ladder about. But when Nani began the story of the year the kitchen curtains caught a spark on Diwali, he stopped, sat on the ladder and laughed the hardest. At lunch he asked Ma, 'If I finish the fans and the balcony by four, can I have the evening?' Ma agreed. He finished at 3:45. I don't know what he was thinking, but he was humming by then.

qa.q: What time did Naveen finish?
qa.a: He finished at 3:45.

qa.q: What was Naveen feeling while he grumbled and banged the ladder about?
qa.a: He felt annoyed and frustrated at losing his plans, though Nani's story soon pulled him back into the family fun.

qa.q: What was smart about Naveen's deal with Ma?
qa.a: He offered to finish specific jobs by a set time in exchange for his evening, so both the festival work and his own plans were respected.

qa.q: How did Charu see Naveen's mood change through the day?
qa.a: Charu noticed him go from loud grumbling to laughing at Nani's story to humming, though she couldn't be sure what he thought.

grounding: Shows a teenager pulled into festival cleaning while wanting time with friends, grumbling yet belonging, and asking for his own evening in return for sharing the work.

passage:
Tuesday: Ganpati arrives on Friday, and Mahima Kaku has a list. Tejas cleans the puja room, runs to the market twice, and strings the marigolds. Tejas, fifteen, had planned a gaming night with friends. He mutters, 'Why is it always me?'
Friday: Tejas stands in the crowded hall during the aarti, cymbals ringing, smelling the modaks he helped carry. Kaku catches his eye and mouths, 'Thank you.' He grins despite himself.
Sunday: After the immersion, he tells Kaku, 'I liked it. But next year can I have Saturday evening for my friends?' Kaku nods. 'Deal. And your cousin Omi takes the market runs.'

qa.q: What did Tejas have to string?
qa.a: The marigolds.

qa.q: What was Tejas feeling during the aarti on Friday?
qa.a: He felt a warm sense of belonging and quiet pride, grinning when Kaku thanked him despite his earlier grumbling.

qa.q: How did Tejas and Kaku balance duty and personal time?
qa.a: Tejas asked calmly for one evening with friends, and Kaku agreed and shared the market runs with a cousin.

qa.q: How might Mahima Kaku feel hearing Tejas say he liked it?
qa.a: Kaku would likely feel happy and relieved, seeing that the work brought him closer to the family, not only resentment.

grounding: Illustrates a teenager who grumbles about festival chores but also feels he belongs, and then asks for some personal time while the duty is shared.

passage:
The day before Eid, Jamal's phone buzzed for the fifth time. Thabo: "Final's at 3. You coming or what?"

Jamal was elbow-deep in samoosa pastry in his grandmother's kitchen in Fordsburg, with three aunties, two cousins and a radio playing old songs. His mother had already given him the windows, the chairs, and the drive with Dad to fetch Uncle Yusuf.

"Ma, can I go at three? It's the final."

"Tomorrow is Eid, Jamal."

He sulked through two trays. Then his grandmother, folding beside him, hummed the song she always hummed, and he found he was folding in rhythm with her.

At one o'clock he tried again, calmer. "Ma, I'll finish the chairs and fetch Uncle Yusuf by two. Can I go for the second half?"

His mother looked at the full trays, then at him. "Back by six. Eid prayers are early."

He texted Thabo: "Second half. Save me a spot."

qa.q: When is the soccer final?
qa.a: The final's at 3.

qa.q: What mixed feelings did Jamal have in the kitchen?
qa.a: Jamal felt frustrated at missing the final and sulked, yet felt a quiet belonging when he found himself folding in rhythm with his grandmother.

qa.q: Why did Jamal's second request work?
qa.a: He asked calmly, offered to finish his jobs first, and asked only for the second half, so the duty got done and some personal time was granted.

qa.q: How might Jamal's mother see his request?
qa.a: She saw he had helped and would finish his tasks, so she could let him go while protecting the family's early Eid morning.

grounding: Shows a teenager pulled into festival cooking and chores while wanting to see friends, grumbling yet belonging, and asking calmly for some time.

passage:
At the community hall behind the masjid, Irfan had been stacking plastic chairs since four. Chand Raat meant a hundred and fifty people, and every teenager in the lane had been drafted.

His phone lit up. Lalit: "Movie at 7, everyone's going. Come na."

Irfan groaned. "Abbu, can I go at six?"

"Who will serve the sherbet?" said Abbu, without looking up from the rice pots.

Irfan carried the jugs, sulking, until old Khala Jaan, who had known him since he was born, patted his cheek and said, "You pour exactly like your Dada did." He didn't know what to do with that. He poured more carefully.

At seven, Lalit's friends posted photos from the cinema. Irfan was ladling sherbet into a line of kids' glasses.

Walking home under the fairy lights, he told Abbu, "Next year I'll do the chairs and the sherbet. But I want Eid evening with my friends."

Abbu nodded. "Deal."

qa.q: How many people come on Chand Raat?
qa.a: Chand Raat meant a hundred and fifty people.

qa.q: What did Irfan feel when Khala Jaan said he pours like his Dada?
qa.a: Irfan felt unexpectedly moved and a little unsure, a flash of belonging that made him pour more carefully.

qa.q: What deal did Irfan make, and why is it fair?
qa.a: He'll do the chairs and sherbet next year but keep Eid evening for friends; the duty is shared and personal time is asked for openly.

qa.q: How might Abbu see Irfan's request on the walk home?
qa.a: Abbu accepts it easily, since Irfan helped all evening and asked clearly for next year.

grounding: Shows a teenager drafted into festival duty while friends go out, grumbling and belonging at once, then asking openly for his own time.

passage:
Hi Kamal bhaiya,

Diwali report from Indore, as promised.

Week one: cleaned the whole house, including the loft, which had a dead lizard in it. Week two: made four hundred shakkarpara with Mummy and Nani. Diwali day: visited eleven relatives' houses. Eleven. I said "Happy Diwali, Aunty" so many times my jaw hurts.

I'd wanted just one day to sleep and go to Nishant's to try his new game. Every time I asked, it was "After Bhai Dooj."

So on Thursday I asked properly, at breakfast. "Mummy, I'll do all the visits tomorrow without complaining, but can I have Saturday off?" She said yes. I think she was shocked I asked nicely.

Weird part: at the last house, Dadi's old friend gave me the same besan laddoo she gave me when I was five, and I nearly cried. I don't know why.

Miss you at these things. Send photos of your Toronto Diwali.

Sachin

qa.q: How many relatives' houses did Sachin visit on Diwali day?
qa.a: Sachin visited eleven relatives' houses.

qa.q: What did Sachin feel on being given the same besan laddoo?
qa.a: Sachin felt a rush of nostalgia, nearly crying without knowing why, remembering being five.

qa.q: What worked when Sachin asked for time off?
qa.a: Asking calmly at breakfast and offering to do the visits without complaint in exchange for Saturday off.

qa.q: How might Mummy have felt at Sachin's calm request?
qa.a: Mummy seemed surprised and pleased by the polite ask, and happily agreed.

grounding: Shows a teenager grumbling through festival cleaning, cooking and visits, feeling real belonging, and asking for a day of personal time.

passage: Avni, you asked why I disappeared all Diwali week, so listen. I'm Preeti, sixteen, and in our house Diwali starts ten days early with cleaning. Every cupboard. Every fan. I was supposed to go to the movie with you all on Thursday, remember? Mummy said, "Movie? Who'll clean the kitchen shelves?" I sulked. I scrubbed those shelves like they'd insulted me. Then Friday we made chaklis with Nani, and she told stories about Diwali in her village, and I laughed so much I forgot I was angry. That's the confusing part. I hated the work and I loved being in it. So on Saturday I tried something new. I said, "Mummy, I'll do all the diyas and the rangoli, but can I have Sunday evening with my friends?" She looked surprised, then said yes. So Sunday, I'm yours, Avni.

qa.q: What did Preeti offer to do in exchange for Sunday evening?
qa.a: All the diyas and the rangoli.

qa.q: How did Preeti feel during Diwali week?
qa.a: Preeti felt resentful and grumpy about the cleaning, but also happy and close to family while making chaklis with Nani.

qa.q: What worked about Preeti's request on Saturday?
qa.a: She offered to share some festival duty and calmly asked for specific personal time, which made it easy for Mummy to say yes.

qa.q: How might Avni have felt when Preeti disappeared all week?
qa.a: Avni was probably a bit disappointed and confused about the missed movie, and pleased to hear Preeti had kept Sunday for friends.

grounding: It illustrates a teenager pulled into festival duties while wanting time with friends, who feels both grumbling and belonging and asks for personal time.
